A · What a Filter Does Key Terms — Saying What You Want

Filter

/ˈfɪl.tər/

Anything that changes how strong each frequency is. A decision about frequencies, carried out on samples.

สิ่งที่เปลี่ยนความแรงของแต่ละความถี่ — คือ "การตัดสินใจเรื่องความถี่" ที่ลงมือทำกับ sample

Passband / stopband

/ˈpɑːs.bænd/

The frequencies you keep, and the frequencies you remove.

ย่านที่เก็บไว้ (passband) กับย่านที่ตัดทิ้ง (stopband)

Cutoff frequency (fc​)

/ˈkʌt.ɒf/

The border between keeping and removing. The shape says which side is removed; the cutoff says where.

เส้นแบ่ง "เก็บ" กับ "ตัด" · ทรงบอกว่าตัดฝั่งไหน cutoff บอกว่าตัดตรงไหน

Gain, in decibels

/ɡeɪn/ · dB

How much a frequency is multiplied by. 0 dB = unchanged · −20 dB = one tenth · −60 dB = one thousandth.

ตัวคูณของแต่ละความถี่ · 0 dB = เท่าเดิม · −20 dB = เหลือ 1/10 · −60 dB = เหลือ 1/1000

🔑

Sessions 6 and 7 gave you a way to see which frequencies are present. A filter is what you do next: decide which of them survive. Everything in this session is that one idea.

1 / 44
A · What a Filter Does Four shapes cover almost every job you will meet
🎛️

Read every picture the same way: curve at the top (0 dB) → that frequency passes; curve at the bottom → it is gone. The dashed line is the cutoff: the shape says which side is removed, the cutoff says where — and a band needs two. Shape + cutoff is how you name a filter.

1 / 44
A · What a Filter Does The job picks the filter — not the other way round
🗣️

Say the job as one sentence and it names the filter: "the hum is at 50 Hz, my signal is above it" → highpass, cutoff above 50 and below the signal (120 Hz here) · "speech lives between 300 and 3400 Hz" → bandpass with those edges · "the reading jitters, the real thing changes slowly" → lowpass. Get the sentence right and the code is one line.

1 / 44
A · What a Filter Does 🌍 The fourth shape: the 50 Hz that is in every clinical recording
🏥

Here the wanted signal lives on both sides of the hum, so a highpass would delete the ECG itself — the sentence is "remove one narrow band, keep everything else" → bandstop. Notice what it did not do: the R peaks are still where they were. Removing one frequency is not the same as damaging the signal.

1 / 44
A · What a Filter Does ↩ What did the filter have to know?

Nothing about hum, and nothing about voices. The filter only ever knew a shape and a border — and neither of them mentions what the signal is.

That is why the same tool cleans an ECG, a phone call and a vibration sensor: you supply the meaning, the filter supplies the arithmetic.

⚠️

And it is why a filter can quietly destroy your data: if part of what you care about lives in the stopband, it is gone, and nothing in the output says so.

A · What a Filter Does 💻 LAB — Design three filters in three lines
①Ask for each shape by name · ② look at what came back · ③ find the cutoff on the plot
lab_a.pyColab · no downloads needed
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal
fs = 8000
designs = {
    "lowpass" : signal.firwin(61, 800, fs=fs),
    "highpass": signal.firwin(61, 800, fs=fs, pass_zero=False),
    "bandpass": signal.firwin(61, [600, 1600], fs=fs, pass_zero=False),
}
for name, h in designs.items():
    w, H = signal.freqz(h, fs=fs)
    plt.plot(w, 20*np.log10(abs(H)+1e-9), label=name)
plt.ylim(-80, 5); plt.xlabel("Hz"); plt.ylabel("dB"); plt.legend(); plt.show()
✅

Three curves with the shapes from slide 6, and the lowpass and highpass cross at the 800 Hz you asked for. Look at what firwin returned: 61 numbers. That short list is the entire filter — and it is where topic B starts.

A · What a Filter Does 🔍 Explore — move the cutoff and watch the wall move
explore_a.pyColab · complete, run as is
for fc in [200, 800, 2000, 3500]:
    h = signal.firwin(61, fc, fs=fs)                       # same length every time
    w, H = signal.freqz(h, worN=8192, fs=fs)
    plt.plot(w, 20*np.log10(abs(H) + 1e-9), label=f"cutoff {fc} Hz")
plt.ylim(-80, 5); plt.xlabel("Hz"); plt.ylabel("dB"); plt.legend(); plt.show()
🔎

Four walls, at 200 · 800 · 2000 · 3500 Hz — the wall goes where you ask. Now look at what did not change: every wall has the same slope. How steep a filter is comes from something else — the number of taps — and that is topic B.

A · What a Filter Does 🎯 Your Turn — translate three sentences into three filters
🎯 Predict first: for each job, say the shape out loud before you look at the code.
your_turn_a.pyColab · complete, run as is
fs = 8000
jobs = {                                                  # sentence -> shape -> cutoff
    "1 rumble below 40 Hz"   : signal.firwin(101, 60, fs=fs, pass_zero=False),          # highpass
    "2 motor whine 1000-1200": signal.firwin(101, [950, 1250], fs=fs, pass_zero=False),  # bandpass
    "3 noise above 30 Hz"    : signal.firwin(101, 30, fs=fs),                            # lowpass
}
for name, h in jobs.items():
    w, H = signal.freqz(h, worN=8192, fs=fs)
    plt.plot(w, 20*np.log10(abs(H) + 1e-9), label=name)
plt.xlim(0, 2000); plt.ylim(-80, 5); plt.xlabel("Hz"); plt.legend(); plt.show()
w, H = signal.freqz(jobs["2 motor whine 1000-1200"], worN=8192, fs=fs)   # 4: whine drifts to 1300?
print("motor filter at 1300 Hz:", round(20*np.log10(abs(H[np.argmin(abs(w - 1300))])), 1), "dB")
✅

1 highpass ≈ 40–60 Hz · 2 bandpass ≈ 950–1250 Hz · 3 lowpass ≈ 30 Hz. The last print is the real question: at 1300 Hz the motor filter is already at −14.2 dB — a narrow bandpass stops seeing what it was built to watch the moment that moves. A tight filter is a bet that the frequency stays put; say so in the report.

B · The Filter Is a List of Numbers Key Terms — The Filter Itself

FIR

/ˌef.aɪˈɑːr/ · Finite Impulse Response

A filter whose output is a weighted sum of the last N inputs. Feed it one spike and the answer stops after N samples — hence "finite".

ฟิลเตอร์ที่เอา input ย้อนหลัง N ตัวมาถ่วงน้ำหนักบวกกัน · ป้อน impulse เข้าไป ผลจะจบใน N sample

Taps (h[k])

/tæps/

The list of weights. Choosing them is designing the filter — there is nothing else to choose. For an FIR filter the taps are exactly its impulse response, Session 3's h[n].

ชุดตัวเลขน้ำหนัก · การเลือกค่าพวกนี้คือการออกแบบฟิลเตอร์ · สำหรับ FIR มันคือ impulse response (h[n] ของคาบ 3) เป๊ะ ๆ

Frequency response

/rɪˈspɒns/

The gain the filter applies at every frequency — the curve you have been reading since slide 6. It is the spectrum of the taps.

ค่าที่ฟิลเตอร์คูณเข้าไปในแต่ละความถี่ — คือเส้นกราฟที่ดูมาตั้งแต่สไลด์ 6 · มันคือสเปกตรัมของ taps

freqz

/frek-zed/

The function that turns taps into that curve. Two lines of code, and it needs no input signal at all.

ฟังก์ชันที่เปลี่ยน taps เป็นเส้นกราฟ · ใช้สองบรรทัด และไม่ต้องมีสัญญาณจริงเลย

🔑

Read the first two cards together: the filter, its taps and its impulse response are three names for the same list of numbers.

B · The Filter Is a List of Numbers This is Session 3, with the coefficients chosen on purpose
y[n]=∑k=0N−1​h[k]x[n−k]

"take the last N inputs, multiply each by its weight, add them up"

Session 3 wrote this and called it convolution.
Session 4 set every h[k] to 1/N and called it a moving average.
Session 8 asks the only question left: what if we choose the weights?

1 / 44
B · The Filter Is a List of Numbers Four lists of numbers, four different filters
🎯

Two of these you already know. All-equal taps are Session 4's moving average — and averaging removes high frequencies: column one is a lowpass. [1, −1] subtracts the previous sample, so it only reacts to change: column two is a highpass. Columns three and four were designed by a library, but they are the same kind of object — a short list of numbers.

1 / 44
B · The Filter Is a List of Numbers How to check a filter: the response is Session 6 applied to h
🔗

Take the DFT of the taps and you have the frequency response — that is the entire definition; freqz just picks the frequency points for you. So the habit of this session: you do not learn what a filter does by running it on your data and squinting. You plot its response first, before any data exists.

B · The Filter Is a List of Numbers ↩ Where have you seen this operation before?

You have been running FIR filters since Session 3. Convolution is the machine; the taps are the instructions you give it.

What is new in this session is not the arithmetic — it is that we now choose h to get a stated effect on frequency, and can check that we got it.

💡

Which is also why "FIR" is not a scary word: if you can write a for-loop over a window, you can implement any FIR filter that exists.

1 / 44
B · The Filter Is a List of Numbers 💻 LAB — Prove the taps and the impulse response are the same list
①Design a filter · ② feed it a single 1 · ③ compare what comes out with the taps
lab_b.pyColab · no downloads needed
import numpy as np
from scipy import signal

h = signal.firwin(7, 1000, fs=8000)
impulse = np.zeros(20); impulse[0] = 1

out = signal.lfilter(h, 1, impulse)          # run the filter on one spike
print("taps  ", np.round(h, 4))
print("output", np.round(out[:7], 4))
print("identical?", np.allclose(out[:7], h), "| zero after that?",
      np.allclose(out[7:], 0))
✅

Both prints show [0.0085 0.0698 0.245 0.3535 0.245 0.0698 0.0085] and then identical? True | zero after that? True. That "zero after that" is the F in FIR: the filter's memory of any one sample runs out after 7 steps.

1 / 44
B · The Filter Is a List of Numbers 🔍 Explore — three lists written by hand, and what each one does
explore_b.pyColab · complete, run as is
x = np.array([0,0,4,4,4,4,0,0,0], dtype=float)            # one step up, one step down
taps = {"average 3": np.ones(3)/3, "difference": np.array([1., -1.]),
        "pass-through": np.array([1.])}
for name, h in taps.items():
    print(f"{name:12s}", np.round(np.convolve(x, h)[:9], 2))
    w, H = signal.freqz(h, worN=512, fs=8000)
    plt.plot(w, abs(H), label=name)                        # gain, not dB: read it straight
plt.xlabel("Hz"); plt.ylabel("gain"); plt.legend(); plt.show()
🔎

Prints — average 3: [0 0 1.33 2.67 4 4 2.67 1.33 0] · difference: [0 0 4 0 0 0 −4 0 0] · pass-through: unchanged. And the plot says the same thing in frequency: the average is a lowpass, the difference a highpass, pass-through a flat line at 1. Smoothing and edge-finding are the same operation with different weights.

B · The Filter Is a List of Numbers 🎯 Your Turn — write the taps for a job, then check them
🎯 Predict first: what should the three weights be if the middle sample matters twice as much as its neighbours?
your_turn_b.pyColab · complete, run as is
x = np.array([0,0,4,4,4,4,0,0,0], dtype=float)
h_mine = np.array([0.25, 0.5, 0.25])            # 1: middle weight double, sums to 1
h_avg  = np.ones(3)/3; h_curv = np.array([-1., 2., -1.])     # 3
print("weighted ", np.round(np.convolve(x, h_mine)[:9], 2))
print("curvature", np.round(np.convolve(x, h_curv)[:9], 2))
for name, h in [("weighted", h_mine), ("average 3", h_avg)]:   # 2
    w, H = signal.freqz(h, worN=512, fs=8000)
    plt.plot(w, 20*np.log10(abs(H) + 1e-9), label=name)
plt.ylim(-40, 3); plt.legend(); plt.show()
print("sum of taps:", h_mine.sum(), h_avg.sum(), h_curv.sum())   # 4: = gain at 0 Hz
✅

1 [0.25, 0.5, 0.25] gives [0 0 1 3 4 4 3 1 0] · 2 yours falls more gently, so it distorts the passband less · 3 [-1, 2, -1] gives [0 0 −4 4 0 0 4 −4 0]: it reacts to curvature, so flat and straight-sloping stretches give zero · 4 prints 1.0 1.0 0.0 — the one to remember: taps summing to 1 leave a constant untouched (gain 1 at 0 Hz); summing to 0 delete it (gain 0 at 0 Hz). The DC gain is readable straight off the taps.

🌍 In the real world

Both filters removed the same frequencies. So why does only one of them still look like the input?

1 / 44
C · The Price You Pay Key Terms — What a Filter Costs

Linear phase

/ˈlɪn.i.ər feɪz/

Every frequency is delayed by the same number of samples, so the waveform keeps its shape. Symmetric taps guarantee it.

ทุกความถี่ถูกหน่วงเท่ากันหมด รูปทรงคลื่นจึงคงเดิม · taps สมมาตร (อ่านกลับหลังได้เหมือนเดิม) รับประกันข้อนี้

Group delay

/ɡruːp dɪˈleɪ/

How long the filter holds the signal up: (N−1)/2 samples for a symmetric FIR. Known exactly, so it can be undone.

ฟิลเตอร์หน่วงสัญญาณนานเท่าไร = (N−1)/2 sample · รู้ค่าแน่นอน จึงหักลบคืนได้

IIR · feedback

/ˌaɪ.aɪˈɑːr/ · Infinite Impulse Response

A filter that feeds its own output back in — uses y[n−1] to compute y[n]. One spike can echo forever, hence "infinite".

ฟิลเตอร์ที่ป้อน output ของตัวเองกลับเข้าไป · ป้อน 1 ตัวเดียว ผลอาจไม่จบเลย

Stability

/stəˈbɪl.ɪ.ti/

Whether that echo dies away or grows without limit. FIR filters cannot be unstable; IIR filters can.

เสียงสะท้อนจะค่อย ๆ หายไปหรือโตไม่หยุด · FIR ไม่มีทางพัง แต่ IIR พังได้

🔑

So far everything was about how loud each frequency comes out. This topic is about when — and what that costs.

1 / 44
C · The Price You Pay Symmetric taps in, every frequency delayed the same — shape survives
🪞

A waveform is a sum of sinusoids (Session 5); its shape comes from how they line up in time. Delay them all equally and they still line up — the picture just slides. Symmetric taps do exactly that, and you can check it by eye: the list reads the same backwards. Every filter firwin makes is symmetric.

1 / 44
C · The Price You Pay The price of that: the whole signal arrives late — by a known amount
⏱️

A delay is only a problem when you do not know its size. Here you do: (N−1)/2 samples, the same for every frequency. On recorded data you shift the result back and the alignment is perfect — filtfilt does that for you. In a live system you cannot shift back in time, and the delay becomes a real cost: more taps, more waiting.

1 / 44
C · The Price You Pay The other way to build a filter: let it remember its own answer
🔁

Roughly the same filter from 10 numbers instead of 101. The trick is one extra term: y[n] = 0.1·x[n] + 0.9·y[n−1] — "keep 90% of what I said last time, mix in 10% of what just arrived." Because y[n−1] already contains the whole past, the filter never has to look back at a hundred raw samples. That is an IIR filter, and every smoothing loop in embedded code is this line.

1 / 44
C · The Price You Pay The price of memory: it can run away
💥

An echo in a room: if each reflection is a little quieter, it fades; point a microphone at its own speaker so each pass is a little louder, and you get the screech. Same here — ∣a∣<1 and the echo dies; ∣a∣≥1 and it grows until you get infinities. Nothing warns you. An FIR filter cannot do this: it has no memory of its own output to amplify.

1 / 44
C · The Price You Pay Choosing: two questions settle almost every case
⚖️

① Does the shape of the waveform matter? Yes → FIR: straight phase, known delay. ② Is the arithmetic budget tight — a microcontroller, a battery, a live loop? Yes → IIR: ten numbers instead of a hundred. If both are yes you have a real engineering problem; if neither, use FIR, because it cannot be unstable.

1 / 44
C · The Price You Pay ↩ Why does only one of them still look like the input?

The FIR delayed every frequency by the same 20 samples, so the square wave slid sideways and stayed a square wave. The IIR delayed each frequency by a different amount, and the pieces re-combined into a new shape — even though every magnitude was identical.

That bent phase is one coin the IIR pays for being cheap. The other is that it can run away. No free lunch — only a different bill.

👻

Which is why this is easy to miss: a magnitude plot cannot show it. Two filters with identical response curves can do visibly different things to your data.

1 / 44
C · The Price You Pay 💻 LAB — Check symmetry, then measure the delay
①Test h[k]=h[N−1−k] · ② send in a pulse · ③ find how far the peak moved
lab_d.pyColab · no downloads needed
h = signal.firwin(41, 1200, fs=8000)
print("symmetric?", np.allclose(h, h[::-1]))

n = np.arange(160)
x = np.exp(-(n - 40)**2 / 30)                       # one short pulse
y = signal.lfilter(h, 1, x)

print("peak in ", np.argmax(x), "| peak out", np.argmax(y),
      "| predicted shift", (len(h) - 1)//2)
✅

symmetric? True, then peak in 40 | peak out 60 | predicted shift 20. The prediction was made from the tap count alone — no signal required. A filter whose delay you can compute in your head is a filter you can align data with.

1 / 44
C · The Price You Pay 🔍 Explore — one line of IIR, then walk a up to 1 and past it
explore_e.py
x = np.zeros(201); x[0] = 1                    # a longer run this time
for a in [0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 1.0, 1.01]:
    y = signal.lfilter([0.1], [1, -a], x)
    z, p, k = signal.tf2zpk([0.1], [1, -a])
    print(f"a={a:5.2f} | |pole|={abs(p[0]):5.2f} | y[200]={y[-1]:12.4g}"
          f" | {'stable' if abs(p[0]) < 1 else 'UNSTABLE'}")
🔎

After 201 samples: a=0.50 → 6.2e−62 · 0.90 → 7.1e−11 · 0.99 → 0.0134 · 1.00 → 0.1 · 1.01 → 0.73. Read the fourth line: at exactly a=1 the echo never fades and never grows — the filter has become an accumulator. That is the knife edge, and rounding can push real coefficients onto it. Hence the rule is ∣a∣<1, strictly.

1 / 44
C · The Price You Pay 🎯 Your Turn — same spec, both technologies, then choose
🎯 The brief: fs​=8000 Hz, lowpass at 800 Hz, running live on a small microcontroller.
your_turn_e.pyColab · complete, run as is
h_fir = signal.firwin(101, 800, fs=8000)                             # 1
b, a  = signal.butter(4, 800, fs=8000, btype="low")
print("multiply-adds per sample: FIR", len(h_fir), "| IIR", len(b) + len(a) - 1)   # 2
z, p, k = signal.tf2zpk(b, a)
print("IIR |poles| =", np.round(np.sort(abs(p))[::2], 3), "-> stable?", np.all(abs(p) < 1))
for name, num, den in [("FIR", h_fir, 1), ("IIR", b, a)]:           # 3
    w, H = signal.freqz(num, den, worN=1024, fs=8000)
    plt.subplot(1, 2, 1); plt.plot(w, 20*np.log10(abs(H) + 1e-9), label=name)
    plt.subplot(1, 2, 2); plt.plot(w, np.unwrap(np.angle(H)), label=name)
plt.legend(); plt.show()                       # 4: which to ship, and what would change your mind
✅

The IIR needs 9 multiply-adds against the FIR's 101, and its poles have magnitudes 0.795 and 0.544 — comfortably inside the circle, so stable. Its phase bends; the FIR's is straight. For this brief — live, small chip, audio — ship the IIR. What would change your mind: if the output feeds a peak-shape measurement rather than a listener, or if the chip has a hardware multiply-accumulate that makes 101 taps free anyway.

Where you can use this 🌍 Three fields that all reach for the same tool

Every one of them asks: which part of this signal do I want to keep?

🎧

Audio & media

The problem: make a recording usable — remove rumble, hiss, hum, or the noise of the room.

What you learned: every equaliser band is a filter, and noise cancelling is a filter running live on a chip in your ear.

EQ · noise cancelling · voice isolation · crossovers

📟

Sensors & control

The problem: a reading that jitters is useless to a controller, and a reading that lags is dangerous to one.

What you learned: a one-line IIR smoother is the standard answer — and its delay is part of the control loop, so it has to be budgeted.

IMUs · thermocouples · drones · robots

🏥

Medicine

The problem: the diagnosis is in the shape of a waveform, and the wiring is in the way.

What you learned: a bandstop removes the mains hum and a linear-phase design leaves the peaks where a clinician expects them.

ECG · EEG · EMG · pulse oximetry

Where you can use this 🌍 Turning this into your own project

a good topic = a signal with something in it you do not want + a way to show it is gone and the rest survived

"Can I pull my own heartbeat out of a phone-camera video of my fingertip?"

Average the red channel per frame · bandpass 0.7–3 Hz · count the peaks and compare with a real pulse reading.

"How much of the noise in my room recording is the air conditioner?"

Spectrum first to find its band · design a bandstop · report the level before and after, in dB.

"Can a phone accelerometer count my steps if I filter it properly?"

Lowpass to kill the hand tremor · highpass to kill gravity · count peaks and compare with a manual count.

📥

What a good report contains: the response of the filter you used with its cutoff and its length stated, the signal before and after, and one number that got better — a noise level, an error count, a correlation. A picture of a cleaner-looking waveform is not evidence on its own.

Summary Session Summary — and the end of the content
A filter
a decision about which frequencies survive · four shapes, one cutoff · the job names it — and it never knows what the signal is
The list
an FIR filter is Session 3's convolution with h chosen on purpose · the taps, the filter and the impulse response are one list
The check
the response is the spectrum of the taps · plot it before you trust the filter · more taps = a steeper wall, and more work per sample
The shape
symmetric taps delay every frequency equally → the waveform keeps its shape · the price is (N−1)/2 samples of delay, known and undoable offline
The memory
an IIR filter reuses its own output, so ten numbers do a hundred taps' work · the price: the phase bends, and it runs away unless ∣a∣<1
That is the last of the content. What remains is yours: the project — record a signal, look at it with Sessions 6 and 7, change it with Session 8, and report a number that got better.

✎Quick Check — Name That Filter⏱ 2 min

A response is flat at 0 dB from 0 to 300 Hz, falls to −40 dB by 900 Hz, and stays there. (a) What shape is it? (b) Roughly where is the cutoff? (c) A 600 Hz tone goes in at amplitude 1. Roughly what comes out?

✅

(a) Lowpass. (b) The −3 dB point is just past 300 Hz, so the cutoff is around 350 Hz — read it off the curve, do not guess it from the middle of the slope. (c) At 600 Hz the curve is at about −20 dB, which is a factor of ten: amplitude ≈ 0.1. Note it is not zero — "in the stopband" never means "gone", it means "small enough".

🧮Worked Example — Turning a Complaint into a Filter

Given

  • "My EEG recording is unreadable — there is mains buzz all over it."
  • fs = 500 Hz · mains = 50 Hz
  • Brain rhythms of interest: 1–40 Hz

Find

  • the shape, the cutoff, and one sentence of justification
Sentence"the junk is at 50, everything I want is below 40"
Shapejunk above everything wanted → lowpass
Cutoffabove 40, below 50 → pick 45 Hz
Checkis 45 Hz below fs/2 = 250? ✓ (Session 2)
∴ lowpass, fc = 45 Hz — one line of firwin
⚠️

A bandstop at 48–52 Hz is the other valid answer, and better if you also need the band above 50 (slide 8). Either way, notice how close 40 and 50 are: the wall has to be steep, so this filter will need many taps (slide 18).

1 / 44
✎Quick Check — Will This One Blow Up?⏱ 3 min

A colleague sends you three one-line filters. Which of them are safe to run, and how do you know without running any of them?

✅

① safe — the feedback coefficient is 0.8 and |0.8| < 1, so each echo is smaller than the last. ② unsafe — |−1.1| > 1, so every pass is 10% louder and it grows without limit. ③ safe, and not even a question — look carefully: there is no y[n−1] term at all, so it is an FIR filter, and no FIR filter can be unstable.

📋The Case — A Wrist Heart-Rate Monitor

The situation

  • An optical sensor on the wrist samples at fs = 100 Hz.
  • A heartbeat is 0.7–3 Hz (42–180 bpm).
  • The signal drifts slowly as the strap shifts: below 0.5 Hz.
  • Arm movement adds bursts above 5 Hz.
  • It runs on a coin cell, and must show the rate live.

Answer these

  • Q1 — which filter shape removes both problems at once, and with what edges?
  • Q2 — an FIR at this fs​ needs about 301 taps to be sharp enough. What delay is that, in seconds?
  • Q3 — is that delay acceptable for a live heart-rate display? Say why.
  • Q4 — FIR or IIR for this product? Give the two reasons that decide it.
💭

Work in order: what to remove → what shape → how sharp → what that costs in delay and arithmetic → which technology fits the product.

✔Part A — Answers
Q1Drift is below the beat, movement is above it → bandpass, about 0.5–5 Hz.
One filter, both problems, because the wanted band sits between them.
Q2(301−1)/2 = 150 samples ÷ 100 Hz = 1.5 seconds.
Q3Borderline, and probably not. The number on the screen would be describing
your heart 1.5 s ago — harmless while resting, wrong during intervals.
Q4IIR. ① The battery: 9 multiply-adds per sample instead of 301.
② Nothing here reads waveform shape — we only count peaks — so the
bent phase costs nothing. Both of the FIR's advantages are irrelevant here.
🧠

Q4 is the habit to carry into the project: the right filter is not the best filter, it is the one whose costs your application does not care about. Change the product to a clinical ECG that a cardiologist reads, and the same reasoning flips to FIR.

💻Q5 — The Filter Chain You Would Ship
case.pyColab · complete, run as is
fs = 100; t = np.arange(0, 30, 1/fs)
x = (np.sin(2*np.pi*1.2*t) + 1.5*np.sin(2*np.pi*0.2*t)          # pulse + drift
     + 1.2*np.sin(2*np.pi*8*t) * ((t % 6) < 1))                  # + movement bursts
b, a = signal.butter(4, [0.5, 5], fs=fs, btype="band")          # 1
z, p, k = signal.tf2zpk(b, a); print("max |pole| =", round(abs(p).max(), 3))    # 2
w, H = signal.freqz(b, a, worN=4096, fs=fs)                      # 3
plt.subplot(1, 2, 1); plt.plot(w, 20*np.log10(abs(H) + 1e-9)); plt.xlim(0, 10)
plt.subplot(1, 2, 2); plt.plot(t, x); plt.plot(t, signal.lfilter(b, a, x)); plt.show()
for name, y in [("lfilter", signal.lfilter(b, a, x)), ("filtfilt", signal.filtfilt(b, a, x))]:
    pk, _ = signal.find_peaks(y, distance=int(0.4*fs), height=0.3)             # 4, 5
    print(f"{name:8s} {len(pk)} peaks in 30 s -> {len(pk)/30*60:.0f} bpm")
_, gd = signal.group_delay((b, a), w=[1.2], fs=fs)
print("lfilter is", round(gd[0]/fs, 2), "s late; filtfilt cancels that with future samples")
✅

Expected: max |pole| ≈ 0.99 — stable but close to the edge, normal for a narrow low-frequency band and the reason production code uses sos form. Drift and bursts vanish; both runs count 36 peaks in 30 s = 72 bpm. The last line is the difference: lfilter delivers each beat 0.26 s late (the group delay at 1.2 Hz); filtfilt cancels that — but a watch cannot, because filtering backwards needs data from the future.
